canonical_topic: Major pollutant categories from power plant combustion
definition: The author identifies six named byproducts of fossil fuel combustion: carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, sulfur oxides, heavy metals, and fly ash/soot, distinguishing which arise from the oxidation reaction versus from impurities in the fuel.
core_idea: Power plants produce five main pollutant categories (CO2, NOx, SOx, heavy metals, fly ash/soot); the first three come from the oxidation chemistry of combustion, while heavy metals and fly ash come from particles physically trapped in the fuel.
key_points: Carbon dioxide (CO2): a nontoxic, odorless, naturally-occurring atmospheric gas and a core byproduct of burning any plant-based fuel; large volumes strengthen the greenhouse effect.

Carbon monoxide (CO): forms from incomplete combustion (insufficient oxygen); it is poisonous because it binds strongly to hemoglobin and interferes with breathing; it can also combine with NOx or SOx to form acid rain.
Nitrogen oxides (NOx, commonly NO2): a mix of nitrogen and oxygen compounds and a major contributor to acid rain.
Sulfur oxides (SOx, commonly SO2): a mix of sulfur and oxygen compounds and a major contributor to acid rain.
Heavy metals (e.g., mercury, lead, plutonium): highly toxic, trapped in the original fuel and released on combustion; they accumulate in living organisms and are difficult for the body to eliminate.
Fly ash/soot: inert particulate matter (fine sand grains or unburned coal) trapped in the fuel; small enough to be inhaled, causing lung damage and diseases such as silicosis.
relationships: CO2, NOx, and SOx result from the oxidation process of combustion itself; heavy metals and fly ash/soot result from impurities physically trapped in the fuel.
trading_implications: Different pollutants are regulated differently (e.g., particulate/metal controls at the plant vs. aggregate CO2 accounting), which can affect compliance costs and fuel choice for generators.
caveats: CO2 and CO are easily conflated, but CO2 is a normal, nontoxic combustion product while CO specifically signals incomplete combustion and is acutely poisonous.
